weekday.title: Weekday
weekday.body:
Day of the week for the converted instant (Time.readable.weekday and weekday_name).

Format: English name + number in parentheses. MontuPython convention: 1 = Sunday … 7 = Saturday.

Examples: Friday (6), Wednesday (4).

spice.title: Gregorian proleptic (human)
spice.body:
Human-readable proleptic Gregorian date in SPICE / NASA style (Time.readable.datespice). The proleptic Gregorian calendar extends Gregorian rules backward without the historical Julian–Gregorian transition.

Format

  • CE: YYYY A.D. MM-DD HH:MM:SS.μμ
  • BCE: YYYY B.C. MM-DD HH:MM:SS.μμ (year shown as historical BCE count)
  • Month and day are MM-DD (not ISO order)
  • Fractional seconds use two or four digits after the decimal point

Examples

  • 2026 A.D. 03-07 14:30:00.0000 — 7 March 2026, 14:30 CE
  • 2781 B.C. 06-27 00:00:00.00 — caniucular datum region (BCE 2782-07-20 input)
  • 0100 B.C. 03-15 06:00:00.00 — 15 March 100 BCE

proleptic.title: Gregorian proleptic (astronomical)
proleptic.body:
Proleptic Gregorian date in the astronomical year convention (Time.readable.datepro): year 0 = 1 BCE, year −1 = 2 BCE, etc. Useful for continuous calculations without a gap at year 1.

Format

  • YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.ffff for CE dates
  • -YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.ffff for BCE dates (leading minus on the astronomical year)
  • ISO-like ordering: year, month, day, then 24-hour time

Examples

  • 2026-03-07 14:30:00.0000 — 7 March 2026 CE
  • -2780-06-27 00:00:00.0000 — astronomical year −2780 (= 2781 BCE)
  • -0001-01-01 00:00:00.0000 — 1 BCE (astronomical year 0 is 1 BCE in historical terms)

mixed.title: Mixed Julian/Gregorian
mixed.body:
Calendar date in the mixed convention (Time.readable.datemix): Julian calendar before 15 October 1582, Gregorian from the reform onward. This is the usual choice for real historical dates.

Format

  • YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS for CE dates
  • -YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS for BCE dates (minus prefix on astronomical year)
  • Month lengths follow the active calendar (Julian or Gregorian) for that date

Examples

  • 2026-03-07 14:30:30 — modern date (Gregorian rules)
  • 1582-10-04 00:00:00 — last Julian day before the 1582 reform (in affected countries)
  • -2780-07-20 00:00:00 — ancient date under Julian rules (near the caniucular datum)

caniucular.title: Caniucular (Egyptian civil)
caniucular.body:
Date in the Egyptian civil (caniucular) calendar (Time.readable.datecan): Horus year, month, season, and day. The year begins with the heliacal rise of Sirius (Sothis); the epoch is hrw 0-I-Akhet-1 = BCE 2782-07-20.

Format

  • hrw HYEAR-MONTH-SEASON-DAY
  • HYEAR — year of Horus (integer, may be negative in display)
  • MONTH — Roman numeral I–IV within the season
  • SEASON — Akhet, Peret, Shemu, or Mesut (intercalary)
  • DAY — 1–30

Examples

  • hrw 0-I-Akhet-1 — caniucular epoch (datum)
  • hrw 1-I-Akhet-2 — day after the datum in Horus year 1
  • hrw 4809-III-Shemu-25 — 7 March 2026 CE in civil form

jd_utc.title: Julian Day — UTC
jd_utc.body:
Julian Day Number on the UTC scale (Time.jed). Counts days and fraction from the Julian epoch (1 January 4713 BCE, 12:00 TT). A pure number — not a calendar string.

Format

  • Decimal number: integer.fraction
  • Fraction 0.0 = noon at the beginning of that JD; 0.5 = midnight; add 0.5 to move from noon-based JD to midnight-based conventions if needed
  • Typically shown with 6 decimal places in this table

Examples

  • 2451545.0 — J2000.0 (2000-01-01 12:00 TT ≈ standard epoch)
  • 2461231.5 — noon on a modern Julian day
  • 705863.500000 — caniucular datum region (BCE 2782-07-20)

tt.title: TT ephemeris seconds (J2000)
tt.body:
Ephemeris seconds on the TT (Terrestrial Time) scale, measured from J2000.0 (2000-01-01 12:00 TT). Corresponds to Time.tt. Not a Julian Day — it is a uniform atomic-time-style count used by SPICE and many ephemerides.

Format

  • Decimal seconds (may be negative for dates before J2000)
  • Uniform scale — no leap seconds

Examples

  • 0.0 — J2000.0 epoch
  • 86400.0 — one TT day after J2000.0
  • Large negative values for ancient dates (e.g. near BCE 2782)

et.title: UTC ephemeris seconds (J2000)
et.body:
Ephemeris seconds on the UTC scale, measured from J2000.0. Corresponds to Time.et. In MontuPython: et = tt − deltat.

Format

  • Decimal seconds from J2000.0 (UTC)
  • Differs from TT by Delta-T (Earth rotation effects)

Examples

  • 0.0 — J2000.0 (UTC ephemeris time origin)
  • For any date, typically a few tens of seconds less than the TT value at the same instant (see Delta-T)

delta_t.title: Delta-T (seconds)
delta_t.body:
Difference TT − UTC in seconds (Time.deltat). Accounts for irregular Earth rotation (tidal braking and leap seconds). Required to convert between civil UTC and uniform TT.

Format

  • Decimal seconds (positive in the modern era: TT runs ahead of UTC)
  • Tabulated internally by MontuPython for historical dates

Examples

  • 67.184 — approximate value near 2020 CE
  • 67692.000 — much larger for ancient dates (e.g. BCE 2782), where extrapolation uncertainty is high

julian_gregorian.title: Julian / Gregorian
julian_gregorian.body: Enter a date in the familiar Gregorian-style calendar. Choose BCE or CE, Mixed or Proleptic calendar type, then pick the date and time. Results update automatically as you change any field.

caniucular.title: Caniucular
caniucular.body: Enter a date in the Egyptian civil calendar: Horus year, month (I–IV within the season), season name, and day (1–30). Each season has four months of 30 days.

julian_day.title: Julian Day Number
julian_day.body: Enter a Julian Day Number (UTC scale), optionally with a fractional part for the time of day. Example: 2461231.5 is noon on that Julian day.

historical_dates.title: Historical dates
historical_dates.body: Select a preset date from Egyptology and astronomy literature. See also the full help under Historical dates (input mode) or Historical Date above the preset list for sources, including José Lull’s La astronomía en el antiguo Egipto.

bce.title: BCE
bce.body: Before Common Era. Years are counted historically (1 BCE is followed by 1 CE). MontuPython converts internally to the astronomical year numbering used by the library.

ce.title: CE
ce.body: Common Era (historically “AD”). Use for dates from 1 CE onward in the Julian/Gregorian input form.

mixed.title: Mixed
mixed.body: Use the historically correct calendar rules: Julian calendar before the 1582 reform, Gregorian calendar afterward. Recommended for real historical dates.

proleptic.title: Proleptic
proleptic.body: Extend Gregorian calendar rules backward for the entire timeline. No Julian–Gregorian switch — useful for uniform astronomical or mathematical dating.

date_grid_weekdays.title: Date (gregorian style, proleptic weekdays)
date_grid_weekdays.body:
The month grid is a date picker in Gregorian style. Its weekday columns follow the proleptic Gregorian layout because Qt’s calendar widget and the desktop UI use that convention internally — not necessarily the weekday of your chosen Mixed or BCE calendar rules.

To know the true day of the week for the converted instant, read the Weekday row in the conversion results (from MontuPython).

Example: 1582-10-04 in Mixed (still Julian) was a Thursday — output shows Thursday (5) — but the grid for October 1582 places the 4th under Monday, because the grid uses the proleptic Gregorian alignment for that civil date.

horus_year.title: Horus Year
horus_year.body:
Year in the Egyptian civil calendar counted from the Horus (caniucular) epoch. Year 0 is anchored at the first apokatastasis (hrw 0-I-Akhet-1 = BCE 2782-07-20).

Format

  • Integer (may be negative for years before the epoch in some displays)
  • Appears as the first number in hrw HYEAR-MONTH-SEASON-DAY

Examples

  • 0 — epoch year (datum)
  • 1 — one civil year after the datum
  • 4809 — modern date in Horus years (e.g. 2026 CE)

caniucular_month.title: Month
caniucular_month.body:
Month within the current season in the Egyptian civil calendar. Each season has four months, numbered with Roman numerals I–IV (not the 12 Gregorian months).

Format

  • One of: I, II, III, IV
  • Third field in hrw HYEAR-MONTH-SEASON-DAY

Examples

  • I — first month of the season (days 1–30)
  • IV — fourth and last month of the season
  • hrw 0-I-Akhet-1 — month I of season Akhet at the datum

caniucular_season.title: Season
caniucular_season.body:
Season name in the Egyptian civil calendar. The year is divided into three seasons of 120 days (Akhet, Peret, Shemu), plus an optional intercalary period (Mesut).

Format

  • One of: Akhet, Peret, Shemu, Mesut
  • Akhet — inundation; Peret — emergence; Shemu — harvest; Mesut — epagomenal days (5 days after Shemu IV-30)

Examples

  • Akhet — first season; contains hrw 0-I-Akhet-1
  • Shemu — e.g. hrw 4809-III-Shemu-25 for a modern March date
  • Mesut — epagomenal days 1–5; e.g. day after IV-Shemu-30 is I-Mesut-1

caniucular_day.title: Day
caniucular_day.body:
Day within the current month and season. Regular seasons use days 1–30; the intercalary season Mesut uses days 1–5 only.

Format

  • Integer day in hrw HYEAR-MONTH-SEASON-DAY
  • Range 1–30 (Akhet, Peret, Shemu) or 1–5 (Mesut)

Examples

  • 1 — first day of the month/season block
  • 30 — last day of a regular month (e.g. IV-Shemu-30)
  • 3 on Mesut — third epagomenal day before the new year

caniucular_offset.title: Step day
caniucular_offset.body:
Use − and + to move one civil day backward or forward from the current caniucular date. All input forms and the results table update immediately.

Examples

  • IV-Shemu-30 then + → I-Mesut-1
  • I-Mesut-5 then + → I-Akhet-1 of the next Horus year
  • − reverses the same transitions

julian_day_utc.title: Julian Day (UTC)
julian_day_utc.body:
Julian Day Number on the UTC scale (Time.jed). Enter days and an optional fractional part for the time of day. This is the primary numeric input when converting from JD to all calendar formats.

Format

  • Decimal: integer.fraction
  • Fraction .0 = noon at the start of that JD; .5 = midnight in common conventions

Examples

  • 2451545.0 — J2000.0 epoch
  • 2461231.5 — noon on that Julian day
  • 625307.5 — default sample value in this form

historical_dates.title: Historical Dates
historical_dates.body:
Preset historical dates from the past whose instant is known in more than one calendar system — typically as a Julian/Gregorian date and as an Egyptian civil (caniucular) date, and sometimes with a lunar or documentary context. Select an entry to load it into all input forms and the results table.

Most entries come from the astronomy of ancient Egypt as discussed by the Egyptologist José Lull in La astronomía en el antiguo Egipto (Astronomy in Ancient Egypt, Universitat de València). Page references below are to that book unless noted otherwise.

Presets and sources

  • BCE 2782-07-20 — First apokatastasis (caniucular datum hrw 0-I-Akhet-1); Lull, calendar chapter
  • BCE 1322-07-20 — Second apokatastasis; Lull
  • CE 139-07-20 — Third apokatastasis (Censorinus); Lull, p. 95
  • BCE 559-10-19 — Papyrus Louvre 7848 (civil + lunar dates); Lull, p. 94
  • BCE 238-03-07 — Canopus decree; Lull, p. 76
  • BCE 237-08-23 / BCE 212-08-17 — Edfu temple inscriptions (25-year lunar cycle); Lull, p. 92
  • CE 384-07-23 — Theon of Alexandria, heliacal rise of Sirius; Lull, p. 98
  • BCE 688-06-11 — Papyrus Louvre E3228d (Taharqa, year 3); Lull, p. 105
  • BCE 46-01-01 — Julian calendar reform (Sosigenes); Suetonius, Divus Julius

northward_equinox.title: Northward equinox
northward_equinox.body:
The northward (vernal) equinox: the instant when the Sun crosses the celestial equator moving northward. Day and night are nearly equal in length.

  • Northern Hemisphere: beginning of astronomical spring (primavera)
  • Southern Hemisphere: beginning of astronomical autumn (otoño)

Computed with Sun.next_seasons() via PyEphem.

northern_solstice.title: Northern solstice
northern_solstice.body:
The northern (summer) solstice: the instant when the Sun reaches its maximum declination north of the celestial equator.

  • Northern Hemisphere: beginning of astronomical summer (verano) — longest day of the year
  • Southern Hemisphere: beginning of astronomical winter (invierno) — shortest day of the year

southward_equinox.title: Southward equinox
southward_equinox.body:
The southward (autumnal) equinox: the instant when the Sun crosses the celestial equator moving southward. Day and night are nearly equal in length.

  • Northern Hemisphere: beginning of astronomical autumn (otoño)
  • Southern Hemisphere: beginning of astronomical spring (primavera)

southern_solstice.title: Southern solstice
southern_solstice.body:
The southern (winter) solstice: the instant when the Sun reaches its maximum declination south of the celestial equator.

  • Northern Hemisphere: beginning of astronomical winter (invierno) — shortest day of the year
  • Southern Hemisphere: beginning of astronomical summer (verano) — longest day of the year

new_moon.title: 🌑 New Moon
new_moon.body:
New Moon (new): the Moon is between Earth and the Sun; the illuminated hemisphere faces away from us. The Moon is invisible or barely visible as a thin crescent at dusk/dawn.

One synodic month ≈ 29.5 days from new moon to new moon.

first_quarter.title: 🌓 First Quarter
first_quarter.body: First Quarter (first): the Moon has completed one quarter of its orbit since the last new moon. The eastern half of the disc is illuminated — a half-moon visible in the afternoon and evening sky.

full_moon.title: 🌕 Full Moon
full_moon.body: Full Moon (full): the Moon is opposite the Sun in the sky; the entire near-side disc is illuminated. Rises at sunset, sets at sunrise.

last_quarter.title: 🌗 Last Quarter
last_quarter.body: Last Quarter (last): the Moon has completed three quarters of its orbit since the last new moon. The western half of the disc is illuminated — a half-moon visible in the late night and morning sky.

bce.title: BCE
bce.body: Before Common Era. Enter the historical year as a positive integer (e.g. 1450 for 1450 BCE).

ce.title: CE
ce.body: Common Era. Enter the year as a positive integer (e.g. 2026 for 2026 CE).

gregorian_proleptic.title: Gregorian proleptic
gregorian_proleptic.body:
Human-readable proleptic Gregorian date in SPICE / NASA style (Time.readable.datespice).

Format: YYYY A.D. MM-DD HH:MM:SS.μμ (CE) or YYYY B.C. MM-DD HH:MM:SS.μμ (BCE).

mixed.title: Mixed Julian/Gregorian
mixed.body:
Date in the mixed calendar convention (Time.readable.datemix): Julian before 1582-10-15, Gregorian afterward.

Format: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS (CE) or -YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS (BCE, astronomical year).

season_delta_t.title: ΔT (days after previous season)
season_delta_t.body:
Elapsed time in days since the previous astronomical season event.

  • For the Northward equinox, counted from the previous Southern solstice.
  • For subsequent seasons, counted from the immediately preceding season in the same year.

Based on the difference of Julian Day numbers returned by MontuPython.

quarter_delta_t.title: ΔT (since last quarter)
quarter_delta_t.body:
Elapsed time in days since the previous lunar quarter phase (new, first, full, or last).

For the first quarter listed in the year, counted from the last quarter before 1 January.

Typical values: ~7 days (new → first), ~7 days (first → full), ~7 days (full → last), ~7 days (last → new).

initial_date.title: Initial date (proleptic Gregorian)
initial_date.body:
Start of the ephemeris interval in the proleptic Gregorian calendar using historical BCE/CE years.

Choose BCE or CE, then year, month, and day. Example: 1500 BCE, 1 January is year 1500 before the Common Era — internally converted to astronomical year −1499 for computation.

The chart axis shows astronomical proleptic dates (datepro); the title uses the human-readable SPICE-style form (1500 B.C. 01-01).

bce.title: BCE
bce.body: Before Common Era. Enter the historical year as a positive integer (e.g. 1500 for 1500 BCE).

ce.title: CE
ce.body: Common Era. Enter the year as a positive integer (e.g. 2026 for 2026 CE).

time_span.title: Time span (years)
time_span.body:
Duration of the sample interval in years (not days or months). The module builds an evenly spaced grid from the initial date through this span.

Example: initial date -1500-01-01 and span 10 covers roughly 1500 BCE to 1490 BCE.

num_points.title: Number of points
num_points.body:
How many evenly spaced time steps to compute along the interval. More points give a smoother curve but take longer to calculate.

Minimum: 2. Default in Montu App: 120.

planets.title: Planets (classic)
planets.body:
Select one or more classical wanderers to plot. In antiquity the word planet (Greek planētēs, “wanderer”) included the Sun and Moon along with Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn — seven bodies that move against the fixed stars.

Available here: Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn. Each selection appears as a separate coloured line. Uranus, Neptune, and Earth are excluded.

property.title: Property
property.body: Ephemeris quantity plotted on the Y-axis. The dropdown shows friendly quantity names; the full catalogue is loaded from assets/planet_properties.json.

chart.title: Chart
chart.body:
The initial date in Parameters uses the proleptic Gregorian calendar with historical BCE/CE years — e.g. entering 1500 BCE means the year 1500 before the Common Era.

The chart X-axis and the hover tooltip datestr show proleptic Gregorian dates in astronomical year numbering (e.g. May 12, -1499 = 12 May 1500 BCE; there is no year 0, so 1 BCE = year 0).

The plot title uses the human-readable proleptic form (e.g. 1500 B.C. 01-01).

Hover over any point on the curve to read datestr (proleptic Gregorian, astronomical), Julian day (JD), and the selected property value. Use the rangeslider below the plot to zoom the time axis.

location.title: Observer location
location.body:
The observer's geographic latitude is the only location parameter that affects the target declination calculation. Longitude is not relevant for this module.

Set the location in the 🧭 Observer Location module, or choose a Famous alignment preset above — presets fill coordinates automatically.

famous_alignments.title: Famous alignments
famous_alignments.body:
Load a documented archaeological sky alignment from assets/alignments.json. Selecting a preset fills the observer site, azimuth, elevation, date range, limiting magnitude, and declination tolerance.

Presets include:

  • Khufu north/south shafts — Great Pyramid of Giza (Old Kingdom)
  • Djoser serdab — Step Pyramid at Saqqara (3rd Dynasty)
  • Senenmut TT353 — tomb-temple entrance at Deir el-Bahari (1472–1457 BCE)

azimuth.title: Azimuth
azimuth.body:
Horizontal compass bearing of the alignment direction, measured clockwise from true North.

  • 0° = North (e.g. the northern shafts of the Great Pyramid)
  • 90° = East (objects rise due East only on the celestial equator)
  • 180° = South (southern shafts of the Great Pyramid point here)
  • 270° = West

The azimuth, together with the elevation and the observer latitude, uniquely determines the target declination shown below the inputs.

elevation.title: Elevation (altitude)
elevation.body:
Angle above the horizon [degrees] of the alignment direction.

Examples from the Great Pyramid of Khufu:

  • King's Chamber northern shaft — elevation ≈ 31.7°
  • King's Chamber southern shaft — elevation ≈ 44.5°
  • Queen's Chamber northern shaft — elevation ≈ 39.6°
  • Queen's Chamber southern shaft — elevation ≈ 39.6°

Horizontal (0°) points to the horizon; vertical (90°) points to the zenith.

year_start.title: From (year)
year_start.body:
Start of the search interval. Enter a positive year and select BCE or CE.

The module will sample the stellar catalogue at several epochs between the start and end years, precessing each star's coordinates to the epoch-of-date system.

Default: 2620 BCE — slightly before the accepted construction date of the Great Pyramid (~2 560 BCE).

year_end.title: To (year)
year_end.body:
End of the search interval. Enter a positive year and select BCE or CE.

Default: 2420 BCE — about 140 years after the nominal construction date. Widening this range increases the chance of catching stars whose alignment window overlaps the range.

mag_limit.title: Limiting magnitude (V)
mag_limit.body:
Only stars with a Johnson V-band visual magnitude brighter than or equal to this value are included.

Examples of reference magnitudes:

  • Sirius (brightest star) — V = −1.46
  • Thuban (α Draconis, Great Pyramid alignment) — V ≈ 3.65
  • Naked-eye limit under dark skies — V ≈ 6.5

Lower values (e.g. 2) restrict the search to the very brightest stars; higher values (e.g. 6) include fainter ones but slow computation.

dec_tolerance.title: Declination tolerance
dec_tolerance.body:
Half-width of the declination band around the target [degrees]. A star is reported as aligned when its epoch-of-date declination falls within target ± tolerance.

Rule of thumb:

  • 0.5° ≈ 30 arcminutes — tight constraint, exact alignments only
  • 1° — default in famous-alignment presets
  • 2°+ — wider margin for shaft width and measurement uncertainty

table.title: Results table
table.body:
Lists every star whose precessed declination falls within ±tolerance of the target declination at any sampled epoch.

Columns:

  • Star — proper name (e.g. Thuban) or catalogue name
  • V mag — Johnson V visual magnitude
  • RA at best epoch — right ascension at the year of closest approach, in h m s
  • Dec at best epoch — declination at the year of closest approach
  • Δ Dec — absolute difference between star declination and target
  • Best year — the sampled epoch at which the star was closest to the target declination

map.title: Sky map
map.body:
Mercator sky map at the midpoint epoch of the search range (RA vs declination).

Elements:

  • White circles — bright stars in their precessed positions
  • Gold stars ★ — aligned stars
  • Gold dashed line — target declination
  • Gold shaded band — declination tolerance
  • Blue dotted line — circumpolar limit: stars beyond this declination never set at the observer latitude (northern sites: dec ≥ limit; southern sites: dec ≤ limit).

Hover over any star for name, coordinates, magnitude, and alignment details.

predefined.title: Predefined site
predefined.body:
Search or select an ancient-world location from assets/locations.json. Choosing a site fills latitude, longitude, and altitude automatically.

Default at startup: Thebes (Luxor), capital of ancient Upper Egypt.

decimal.title: Decimal degrees
decimal.body:
Enter coordinates as decimal degrees (DD.dddddd°). Positive latitude = north, negative = south. Positive longitude = east, negative = west.

Example: Luxor → lat 25.6967, lon 32.6422.

sexagesimal.title: Sexagesimal (DMS)
sexagesimal.body:
Enter coordinates as degrees, arcminutes, and arcseconds with a hemisphere letter (N/S for latitude, E/W for longitude). Altitude remains in metres.

Example: 25°41'48.1"N, 32°38'32.0"E.

latitude.title: Latitude
latitude.body: Geodetic latitude of the observing site [degrees]. North positive, south negative. Range: −90° … +90°.

longitude.title: Longitude
longitude.body: Geodetic longitude of the observing site [degrees]. East positive, west negative. Range: −180° … +180°.

altitude.title: Altitude
altitude.body: Elevation above mean sea level in metres. Converted internally to kilometres for montu.Observer. When you click the map, MontuPython queries the free Open-Elevation service.

map_labels.title: Map labels
map_labels.body:
Choose how place names appear on the map tiles.

  • Local names — standard OpenStreetMap tiles (e.g. Arabic in Egypt).
  • English names — Wikimedia internationalized tiles that prefer name:en where available.

Switching reloads the map. Your choice is remembered for future sessions.
